Genes, Populations, & Evolution
¨Causes of Microevolution
¨Genetic Drift
¤Changes in the allele frequencies of a population due to chance rather than selection by the environment
¤Does not necessarily lead to adaptation to the environment
¤Occurs by disproportionate random sampling from population
  nCan cause the gene pools of two isolated populations to become dissimilar
  nSome alleles are lost and others become fixed (unopposed)
¤Likely to occur:
  nAfter a bottleneck
  nWhen severe inbreeding occurs, or
  nWhen founders start a new population
¤Stronger effect in small populations
explanation: Genetic drift is a cause of microevolution defined as changes in the allele frequencies of a population due to random chance, rather than natural selection by the environment. Because it is random, genetic drift does not necessarily result in adaptation. It occurs when alleles are disproportionately sampled from a generation, which can lead to some alleles being completely lost while others become fixed (frequency of 100%, or unopposed). Genetic drift can cause isolated populations to become genetically distinct and has a much stronger effect in small populations. It is highly likely to occur after a population bottleneck, during severe inbreeding, or when a small group of founders establishes a new population.

questions.q: Unlike natural selection, how does genetic drift change allele frequencies?
opts: By favoring traits that provide a survival advantage
By random chance events rather than environmental selection
By increasing the rate of gene flow between populations
By forcing random mating in large populations
questions.exp: Genetic drift changes allele frequencies due to random chance sampling rather than environmental selection, meaning it does not necessarily lead to adaptation.

questions.q: In which type of population does genetic drift have the most significant (strongest) impact?
opts: Populations with high rates of gene flow
Populations that do not experience mutations
questions.exp: Genetic drift has a stronger, more pronounced effect in small populations because random events have a larger relative impact on smaller gene pools.
